title: Deduplicate while preserving order
prompt_md:
Implement `dedupe`, which returns the items of an iterable with duplicates removed and **first-seen order preserved**.

The catch is the complexity bound: the tests include a 200 000-element input with a per-call operation budget. A solution that scans the output list to decide whether it has seen an item will pass the correctness tests and fail the budget one.

Also implement `dedupe_by(items, key)`, the same thing keyed on a derived value — the shape you actually need in production, where two records are "the same" because their ids match rather than because the whole object does.

Both functions must accept any iterable (including a generator that can only be consumed once) and must not require the items to be sortable.
requirements_md: `dedupe(items)` returns a `list` in first-seen order with duplicates removed.
`dedupe_by(items, key)` does the same, treating two items as duplicates when `key(item)` matches.
Both must be O(n) in the number of items — linear, not quadratic.
Both must accept a one-shot iterable (a generator) and consume it exactly once.
Items are hashable but not necessarily orderable; do not sort.
Preserve the *first* occurrence of each duplicate, not the last.

starter_files.content:
"""Order-preserving deduplication.

Both functions must be linear in the number of items.
"""
from collections.abc import Callable, Hashable, Iterable
from typing import Any


def dedupe(items: Iterable[Any]) -> list[Any]:
    """Return the items with duplicates removed, first-seen order preserved.

    >>> dedupe([3, 1, 3, 2, 1])
    [3, 1, 2]
    """
    raise NotImplementedError


def dedupe_by(items: Iterable[Any], key: Callable[[Any], Hashable]) -> list[Any]:
    """Deduplicate on a derived key, keeping the first item per key.

    >>> dedupe_by([{"id": 1, "v": "a"}, {"id": 1, "v": "b"}], key=lambda r: r["id"])
    [{'id': 1, 'v': 'a'}]
    """
    raise NotImplementedError

solution_files.content:
"""Order-preserving deduplication."""
from collections.abc import Callable, Hashable, Iterable
from typing import Any


def dedupe(items: Iterable[Any]) -> list[Any]:
    """Return the items with duplicates removed, first-seen order preserved.

    dict.fromkeys does this in one pass: dicts preserve insertion order and
    ignore a repeated key, which is exactly the semantics required.
    """
    return list(dict.fromkeys(items))


def dedupe_by(items: Iterable[Any], key: Callable[[Any], Hashable]) -> list[Any]:
    """Deduplicate on a derived key, keeping the first item per key.

    A set of seen keys plus one pass. The `seen.add` returning None is why this
    is written as a loop rather than a comprehension with a side effect.
    """
    seen: set[Hashable] = set()
    out: list[Any] = []
    for item in items:
        k = key(item)
        if k not in seen:
            seen.add(k)
            out.append(item)
    return out

tests.name: dedupe removes duplicates and keeps first-seen order
dedupe consumes a generator exactly once
dedupe_by keys on the derived value and keeps the first item
tests.body:
from dedupe import dedupe_by


def test_keeps_the_first_item_per_key():
    rows = [
        {"id": 1, "v": "first"},
        {"id": 2, "v": "other"},
        {"id": 1, "v": "second"},
    ]
    assert dedupe_by(rows, key=lambda r: r["id"]) == [
        {"id": 1, "v": "first"},
        {"id": 2, "v": "other"},
    ]


def test_items_need_not_be_hashable_themselves():
    # dicts are unhashable; only the key has to be.
    rows = [{"id": "a"}, {"id": "a"}]
    assert dedupe_by(rows, key=lambda r: r["id"]) == [{"id": "a"}]


def test_key_is_called_once_per_item():
    calls = []

    def key(item):
        calls.append(item)
        return item

    dedupe_by([1, 1, 2], key=key)
    assert calls == [1, 1, 2]

tests.name: dedupe does not require sortable items
dedupe stays linear on 200k items (operation budget)
tests.body:
"""Reject quadratic solutions without depending on wall-clock speed.

The probe counts equality comparisons. A linear solution hashes each item and
compares only on hash collision, so the count stays close to n. A solution that
tests `item not in out` compares against the accumulated output and lands in the
billions -- the budget below is loose enough to be stable on a shared runner and
tight enough that no quadratic solution can slip through.
"""
import pytest

from dedupe import dedupe, dedupe_by

N = 200_000


class Probe:
    __slots__ = ("value",)
    comparisons = 0

    def __init__(self, value):
        self.value = value

    def __hash__(self):
        return hash(self.value)

    def __eq__(self, other):
        type(self).comparisons += 1
        return isinstance(other, Probe) and self.value == other.value


def test_dedupe_stays_linear():
    items = [Probe(i % (N // 2)) for i in range(N)]
    Probe.comparisons = 0
    result = dedupe(items)
    assert len(result) == N // 2
    budget = 4 * N
    assert Probe.comparisons <= budget, (
        f"{Probe.comparisons} equality comparisons for {N} items exceeds the "
        f"linear budget of {budget}; the solution is scanning a sequence"
    )


def test_dedupe_by_stays_linear():
    rows = [{"id": i % (N // 2)} for i in range(N)]
    out = dedupe_by(rows, key=lambda r: r["id"])
    assert len(out) == N // 2
    assert out[0] == {"id": 0}

hints.md: The bound is the whole exercise. Deciding "have I seen this?" against the output list is O(n) per item; the same decision against a hash-based container is O(1). So you need a second container whose only job is membership.

For `dedupe`, there is a one-liner: dicts preserve insertion order and silently ignore a repeated key, so building a dict from the items and taking its keys *is* order-preserving deduplication. For `dedupe_by` you need the explicit `seen` set, because you are deduplicating on something other than the item itself — and note that a comprehension cannot do it cleanly, since `seen.add(...)` returns `None`.
